newsitem.title: FRANCE: Polisario pins hopes on Baker for W.Sahara peace.
newsitem.headline: Polisario pins hopes on Baker for W.Sahara peace.

text.p: The Polisario Front, seeking independence in the disputed Western Sahara, said it believed U.N. envoy James Baker could relaunch the region's stalled peace plan, Algeria's official news agency APS said on Sunday.

APS quoted Polisario foreign minister Bachir Mustapha Sayed as telling reporters in Tindouf, Algeria, on Saturday that Baker faced a "great challenge" over the U.N. peace plan for the former Spanish colony which is claimed by Morocco.

But Baker's experience as a former U.S. secretary of state, his political weight and his backing by the U.N. Security Council and the international community would enable him to answer the challenge, said Mustapha Sayed.
Baker, on his first tour of North Africa since U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan appointed him his personal envoy for Western Sahara last month, was due in Tindouf later on Sunday.
Algeria is a long-time supporter of the Polisario which has its rear base in Tindouf.

It is also home to thousands of Saharan refugees, many of whom fled years of conflict in Western Sahara before a U.N. ceasefire in September 1991 ended fighting between the Polisario and Moroccan troops.

The second part of a U.N. peace plan, a referendum to enable Saharans to decide whether the territory should be independent or integrate with Morocco, has been held up by disputes over who should be allowed to vote.
The ballot was initially planned for January 1992.
Baker is on a fact-finding trip, which has taken him to Morocco, Algeria and neighbouring Mauritania.
On Saturday, he held talks with Mauritanian President Maaouya Ould Sid'Ahmed Taya after earlier meeting Prime Minister Cheikh El Afia Ould Mohamed Khouna and Foreign Minister Sidi Ould Khalifa.
Mauritanian television, monitored by the British Broadcasting Corporation, quoted Baker as saying he had had "an interesting meeting" with the president.
Baker added: "This visit aims at carrying out a new analysis of the situation in the Western Sahara."
